document.abstract: This paper describes a method of producing scenes for TV programs, using “dynamic 3D human models.” Dynamic 3D human models are 3D models generated from images shot by multiple cameras surrounding an actor for each frame using 3D-reconstruction and texture-mapping techniques. They can provide highly realistic images as well as natural motions without having to use a motion-capture system. In addition, they allow production to be more flexible, enabling the positions of models to be changed or multiplying the amount used. Dynamic 3D human models are therefore suitable for producing crowd scenes. Although techniques of 3D reconstruction and texture mapping have been discussed and several applications have been proposed, they have not been widely introduced into TV or movie production, because of the huge amounts of data and insufficient textural quality. By establishing an efficient production flow with recent powerful computers and 24 HD cameras, the authors succeeded in producing crowd scenes with sufficient quality for a TV program, which will be aired in December 2009. The scenes involving 1,000 soldiers can be produced by shooting several sequences with two actors. The production flow that was established is described as well as scenes that were produced using dynamic 3D human models for a drama.

authors.affiliation: Science and Technical Research Laboratories of NHK (Japan Broadcasting Corp.).
authors.bio: Kensuke Hisatomi currently works in the Science and Technical Research Laboratories of NHK (Japan Broadcasting Corp.). He joined NHK in 1999. From 2003 to 2007, he worked in the Engineering Administration Department of NHK where he was involved in development of digital broadcasting in Japan. He has been in the Science and Technical Research Laboratories since 2007. His research interests include three-dimensional reconstruction and three-dimensional video processing for broadcasting. Hisatomi received B.E. and M.E. degrees in applied physics from Waseda University in 1997 and 1999, respectively.
authors.name: Kensuke Hisatomi

authors.bio: Kimihiro Tomiyama joined NHK in 1998 after receiving B.E. and M.E. degrees from the Tokyo Institute of Technology. He has been with NHK Science & Technical Research Laboratories since 2001, and has researched 3D video coding for broadcasting.
authors.name: Kimihiro Tomiyama

authors.affiliation: Advanced Television systems department of the Science & Technology Research Laboratories of NHK
authors.bio: Miwa Katayama is a principal research engineer in the advanced television systems department of the Science & Technology Research Laboratories of NHK. Her research interests include three-dimensional video systems, image coding, and video applications. Katayama is a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE). She received a B.S. degree from Sophia University in 1990, and M.S. and Ph.D. degrees from Tokyo University in 1992 and 1995, respectively.
authors.name: Miwa Katayama

authors.affiliation: NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories
authors.bio: Yuichi Iwadate is a senior research engineer in the NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories. He received a B.E. degree and a Dr. Eng. degree from Doshisha University, Kyoto, Japan, in 1981 and 1993, respectively. He has been involved in research on HDTV systems, digital transmission systems, and 3D image processing. Currently he is interested in a scene reconstruction method using multiple camera system.
authors.name: Yuichi Iwadate

authors.bio: Koji Matsunaga is a computer graphics supervisor of the drama “sakano-ueno-kumo,” which includes scenes produced by the method described in the paper. He joined NHK in 1990 after graduating Yamaguchi Ube National College of Technology. From 1990 to 1997, he worked as a cameraman at NHK Tottori Broadcasting Station. Matsunaga worked at Tokyo Broadcasting Center of NHK since 1997 as a computer-graphic engineer and a supervisor of video effects, where he is engaged in the visual effects of science programs and dramas.
authors.name: Koji Matsunaga

authors.affiliation: Production and development of computer graphics in the broadcast engineering department of NHK.
authors.bio: Yoshiyuki Ito is currently engaged in the production and development of computer graphics in the broadcast engineering department of NHK. He joined NHK in 2001. From 2001 to 2005, he was a production engineer at NHK Fukui Station. Ito received B.E. and M.E. degrees in information electronics from Nagoya University.
authors.name: Yoshiyuki Ito

authors.bio: Wataru Ishihara is a computer graphics engineer in the broadcast engineering department of NHK. He joined NHK after receiving B.E. degree from Waseda University in 2001. He currently works on computer graphics for broadcasting programs and he is also engaged in the development of the simulation software of the crowd scene.
authors.name: Wataru Ishihara
